lead: A rigid body in plane motion obeys two equations at once: the resultant force sets the acceleration of its mass centre, and the resultant moment about the mass centre sets its angular acceleration. These are Newton's second law and its rotational partner, the Euler equation. They turn a drawing of forces into numbers for a machine part, a rolling drum, or a vehicle. The method is always the same: draw the free-body diagram, draw the kinetic diagram, write the two equations, and solve. This chapter applies that method to translation, fixed-axis rotation and rolling without slip.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for translation and fixed-axis rotation, 6.2 for plane motion, and the mass moment of inertia from Unit 4, Mass Moment of Inertia; Unit 5 gives Newton's second law for particles.

sections.h3: Force, mass centre and angular acceleration

blocks.text: For plane motion, a rigid body has mass m in kg and mass moment of inertia I<sub>G</sub> in kg m² about an axis through its mass centre G, perpendicular to the plane of motion. The acceleration of G is a<sub>G</sub>, with components a<sub>Gx</sub> and a<sub>Gy</sub> in m/s². The angular acceleration is α in rad/s². Pick a positive sense for α and keep it.
ΣF<sub>x</sub> = m a<sub>Gx</sub>,   ΣF<sub>y</sub> = m a<sub>Gy</sub>,   ΣM<sub>G</sub> = I<sub>G</sub> α
blocks.where: ΣF<sub>x</sub> and ΣF<sub>y</sub> are the sums of external force components in N; ΣM<sub>G</sub> is the sum of external moments about G in N m; m is mass in kg; I<sub>G</sub> is the mass moment of inertia about the centroidal axis in kg m²; α is angular acceleration in rad/s².

blocks.text: The force equations say G moves like a particle of mass m under the resultant force. The moment equation says only the resultant moment about G changes the spin. A force whose line of action passes through G has zero moment about G, so it cannot produce α. Internal forces cancel in pairs and do not appear.

For rotation about a fixed axis O, take moments about O: ΣM<sub>O</sub> = I<sub>O</sub> α, where I<sub>O</sub> = I<sub>G</sub> + m d², d is the distance OG in m. This removes the unknown reaction at O from the moment equation. Use either the G set or the O equation, not both as independent equations unless you are checking.

The free-body diagram (FBD) shows the body alone with every external force: weight mg, normal reactions, friction, applied loads, support reactions and applied couples. Do not draw m a<sub>G</sub> or I<sub>G</sub> α on the FBD. Those belong on the kinetic diagram (KD).

items: Choose axes x and y, and mark the positive sense of α.
Draw the FBD with all real forces and couples.
Beside it draw the KD: an arrow m a<sub>G</sub> at G, and a curved arrow I<sub>G</sub> α for angular acceleration.
Write ΣF<sub>x</sub> = m a<sub>Gx</sub>, ΣF<sub>y</sub> = m a<sub>Gy</sub>, ΣM<sub>G</sub> = I<sub>G</sub> α.
Add the kinematic constraint, such as a<sub>G</sub> = r α for rolling without slip.
Solve and check units: N for force, N m for moment, m/s² for a<sub>G</sub>, rad/s² for α.

blocks.text: D'Alembert's principle gives the same equations in equilibrium form. Add an inertia force −m a<sub>G</sub> at G and an inertia couple −I<sub>G</sub> α to the FBD. Then ΣF = 0 and ΣM<sub>G</sub> = 0 for the body plus inertia terms. This is only a bookkeeping trick; the physics is still Newton's second law.

Translation only: α = 0, and every point has the same acceleration a<sub>G</sub>. The moment equation gives ΣM<sub>G</sub> = 0, so the resultant force passes through G when there is no applied couple.

Fixed-axis rotation about O: G moves on a circle of radius d = OG. Its acceleration has a tangential part d α and a normal part d ω², where ω is angular velocity in rad/s. The equation ΣM<sub>O</sub> = I<sub>O</sub> α gives α from the moments about O. The force equations then give the reaction at O.

Rolling without slip on a fixed surface: the contact point has zero velocity at that instant. For a wheel or cylinder of radius r, a<sub>G</sub> = r α and v<sub>G</sub> = r ω, with matching positive senses. The friction force at contact is static and unknown. It is not μN unless slip is just starting. Friction usually supplies the moment that spins the body, so it appears in both the force and moment equations.

items: Force through G: no moment about G, so it translates the body and friction may cause spin.
Force at the rim: has a moment about G and also changes a<sub>G</sub>.
Uniform cylinder rolling under a force at its centre: friction is one third of the applied force; see the worked example.

figure.caption: The diagram shows the working order: free-body diagram of real forces, kinetic diagram of m a_G and I_G α, then the force and moment equations. The moment equation is the one that decides α once the forces are known.

spec.title: Force and acceleration
spec.aria: The force solution goes from a free-body diagram to a kinetic diagram, then to the two Newton-Euler equations and a unit check.

examples.question: A uniform solid cylinder of mass 10 kg and radius 0.20 m rolls without slipping on a horizontal plane. A horizontal force P = 40 N pulls at the centre, parallel to the plane. Find the acceleration of the centre and the static friction force at the contact.
steps: Data: m = 10 kg, r = 0.20 m, P = 40 N. The centroidal mass moment of inertia is I<sub>G</sub> = ½ m r² = ½ × 10 × (0.20)² = 0.200 kg m².
Take +x to the right. P acts at G to the right. Static friction f acts to the left at the bottom contact. Normal reaction N and weight mg are vertical and cancel; there is no vertical acceleration.
Force equation: P − f = m a, where a is the acceleration of G to the right in m/s².
Moment about G: only f has a moment. Friction to the left at the bottom gives a clockwise moment f r. Take clockwise α positive. Rolling without slip gives a = α r, so α = a/r.
Moment equation: f r = I<sub>G</sub> α = I<sub>G</sub> (a/r). Hence f = I<sub>G</sub> a / r² = (0.200/0.0400) a = 5.00 a, with a in m/s² and f in N.
Substitute in the force equation: 40 − 5.00a = 10a. Then 40 = 15a, so a = 2.667 m/s². Also α = a/r = 13.333 rad/s².
examples.answer: The centre accelerates at a = 2.667 m/s² to the right, and static friction is f = 13.333 N to the left.
examples.check:
m = 10.0
r = 0.20
P = 40.0
IG = 0.5 * m * r**2
a = P / (m + IG / r**2)
f = IG * a / r**2
print(round(a, 3))
print(round(f, 3))

traps: Drawing m a<sub>G</sub> or I<sub>G</sub> α on the free-body diagram as if they were real loads. They belong on the kinetic diagram; in D'Alembert form they carry a minus sign.
Taking moments about G but using I<sub>O</sub>, or leaving out the moment of friction about G. Use I<sub>G</sub> for ΣM<sub>G</sub> and I<sub>O</sub> only for ΣM<sub>O</sub>.
Setting rolling friction equal to μN. Static friction in rolling without slip is found from the equations; μN is only the limiting value when slip starts.
Mismatching signs in a<sub>G</sub> = r α. If a<sub>G</sub> is to the right for a wheel rolling right, α is clockwise.
Using ΣF = m a<sub>G</sub> for a point other than G, or ΣM = I α about an accelerating point without the correction term. For general plane motion, write the moment equation about G.

quiz.q: Write the three plane-motion equations about the mass centre G and define each symbol.
quiz.a: ΣF<sub>x</sub> = m a<sub>Gx</sub>, ΣF<sub>y</sub> = m a<sub>Gy</sub>, ΣM<sub>G</sub> = I<sub>G</sub> α; m is mass, a<sub>G</sub> is acceleration of G, I<sub>G</sub> is centroidal mass moment of inertia, α is angular acceleration.

quiz.q: Why can a force through G not change α about G?
quiz.a: Its moment arm about G is zero, so it adds nothing to ΣM<sub>G</sub>. Only a couple or a force with a line of action away from G changes α.

quiz.q: A 5 kg uniform disk of radius 0.10 m rolls without slip on a horizontal plane under a horizontal force P = 15 N at its centre. Find a and the friction force f.
quiz.a: I<sub>G</sub> = 0.5 × 5 × 0.10² = 0.025 kg m². f = I<sub>G</sub> a/r² = 2.5a. Force: 15 − f = 5a gives 15 = 7.5a, so a = 2 m/s² and f = 5 N.

quiz.q: For a uniform cylinder rolling without slip under a horizontal force P at its centre, show that f = P/3 and find f when P = 60 N.
quiz.a: f = I<sub>G</sub> a/r² = (0.5 m r²)a/r² = 0.5m a. Force: P − f = m a gives P = 1.5m a. Hence f = P/3. For P = 60 N, f = 20 N.

quiz.q: State the parallel-axis relation for I<sub>O</sub> in terms of I<sub>G</sub>.
quiz.a: I<sub>O</sub> = I<sub>G</sub> + m d², where d is the distance OG in m.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a free-body diagram and a kinetic diagram?
quiz.a: The FBD shows real external forces and couples. The KD shows the inertia terms m a<sub>G</sub> at G and I<sub>G</sub> α, which represent the motion, not forces applied by other bodies.

quiz.q: A disk rotates about a fixed axis O with I<sub>O</sub> = 0.80 kg m². The net moment about O is 4.0 N m. Find α.
quiz.a: ΣM<sub>O</sub> = I<sub>O</sub> α gives 4.0 = 0.80α, so α = 5.0 rad/s².

quiz.q: A rigid body translates with no rotation. What is ΣM<sub>G</sub>, and where does the resultant force act?
quiz.a: α = 0, so ΣM<sub>G</sub> = 0. With no applied couple, the resultant force must pass through G.

beyond: Not for the exam. In vehicle dynamics, these equations feed tyre and suspension models: the mass-centre equations give body motion and the moment equation gives yaw or pitch. In robotics, the same Newton-Euler form is used link by link to compute joint torques. Search next for 'Newton-Euler rigid body', 'rolling resistance', and 'unsprung mass'.
